item.title: 008. Feeding an army before refrigeration
item.description:
- Pre-refrigeration army food was food pushed below the water-activity line where microbes stop growing: threshed grain, twice-baked biscuit, salt pork and beef, dried meat and pemmican. It kept the calories and lost the vitamin C, which is why scurvy was the limit, mostly at sea. - On land the binding constraint was carrying, not keeping. Animals eat what they haul (Engels's arithmetic, Devereaux's "wagon equation"), so overland supply had a radius of a few days and armies carried about seven to ten days of food; the rest came from water transport, requisition, markets and foraging, in proportions set by season and population density (van Creveld versus Lynn). - Famous cases: Alexander's Gedrosian march (a fleet that didn't arrive), Napoleon's 1812 invasion (wagons, roads, horses and disease broke the army in summer, before the winter), and the Civil War, where the canning industry boomed but the issued ration was still salt pork and hardtack.
Chew on this: 1. The carrier that eats its own cargo shows up in wagons and in rockets. Where else does that pattern appear, and what were the escapes (ships for armies, staging for rockets)? 2. Lind's correct rule (citrus) rode on a wrong mechanism (acid), and the wrong mechanism let the navy swap lemons for limes. Can you think of a rule with a wrong reason that held up fine for centuries, and what made it safe? 3. The seven-to-ten-day buffer keeps appearing, from Engels's Macedonians to Sherman's wagons. What would have to change about the animal, the road, or the food to break it?
Sources: - Grain stored threshed not as flour, Roman contubernium hand mills, Greek hoplite armies lacking them, foraging parties up to a legion, 5 to 15 percent extraction, army size scale: Bret Devereaux, ACOUP, "Logistics, How Did They Do It, Part II: Foraging": https://acoup.blog/2022/07/29/collections-logistics-how-did-they-do-it-part-ii-foraging/ - item.title: 007. The gas fire, part 2: the box
item.description:
- At forging heat the walls heat the steel, mostly by radiation that goes as the fourth power of absolute temperature (Stefan-Boltzmann): walls at 1300 C radiate about 350 kW per square meter, published furnace work puts radiation at 75 to 90 percent of heat to the load, and a 3 inch square door leaks about 2 kW. - Lining is a trade between low stored heat (fiber, about 128 kg/m3) and thermal mass (hard firebrick, about 2,100 kg/m3); hot insulating firebrick conducts no worse than blanket, and fiber heats fast because there is so little of it, not because heat moves slowly through it. Rigidizer and hard coatings earn their keep mechanically (erosion, dust, flux); reflectivity claims are unverified. Fired refractory ceramic fiber (IARC 2B) partly converts to cristobalite and is the real breathing hazard. - Size the burner to the chamber (about one 3/4 inch burner per 300 to 350 cubic inches for normal shapes), bring it in tangentially to avoid a hot spot, and pick venturi, blown or ribbon by need. Forge welds fail on oxide more than on heat; borax dissolves iron oxide into a low-melting glass, and dissolves the refractory floor the same way.
Forge task: Map the chamber. Run the forge at your usual forging pressure and let it soak 20 to 30 minutes. Put four short pieces of the same mild steel (for example 1/2 inch round) on the floor: center, each back corner, just inside the door. Pull them at the same moment after a couple of minutes, lay them side by side in shade and compare colors; note which faced the burner. Then lay one long bar across the floor and watch the color gradient. Sketch the chamber from above and mark the hot spot and cold corners. Repeat at a lower pressure if there's time.
Safety: ventilation and a CO alarm every time; soapy-water leak test on every fitting before lighting, never a flame; propane pools low, natural gas rises. Shaded glasses (about shade 2 to 3) when looking into the chamber, don't stare, and keep your face out of line with the door. Don't brush or poke bare fiber; a crumbling lining is a separate job with a P100 respirator, wetted down, outdoors.
Chew on this: 1. If radiation does most of the work and goes as the fourth power of wall temperature, should your next effort go into a bigger burner or a better box? Which would you test first? 2. A fiber forge heats a blade faster but drops temperature faster when the cold blade goes in. For an even hardening heat, which matters more, and could you get both? 3. If a closed hot box is nearly a blackbody whatever the coating, how would you design a fair test of whether a reflective coating does anything in your forge?
Sources: - Cavity radiation approximating a blackbody, independent of cavity properties: Wikipedia, Black body: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_body - Radiation 75 to 90 percent of heat to the load in high temperature furnaces, about 90 percent in their furnace: Herrera et al., DYNA 88(217), 2021: https://www.redalyc.org/journal/496/49671281031/html/ - High temperature furnaces heat mainly by line-of-sight wall radiation, low temperature ones by convection: The Heat Treat Doctor, Heat Treatment of Fasteners, Tips for Operation: https://www.heat-treat-doctor.com/documents/TipsforEquipOp.pdf - Forced convection in gases 25 to 250 W/m2K (from Incropera): Michigan Tech, typical values of heat transfer coefficient: https://pages.mtu.edu/~fmorriso/cm3120/typical_values_heat_transfer_coefficient.pdf - Kaowool blanket densities, conductivity at mean temperatures, 1260 C classification, 1093 C continuous: Morgan, Kaowool Blankets data sheet: https://www.morganadvancedmaterials.com/media/2975/5-14-205_kaowoolblankets_072018.pdf - K-23 and K-26 insulating firebrick density, conductivity, classification temperatures: Morgan, K IFB series data sheet: https://www.morganthermalceramics.com/media/9429/k-ifb-series_eng.pdf - Kast-O-Lite 30 density, conductivity, 1650 C limit, 55 percent alumina: Kast-O-Lite 30 LI Plus data sheet: https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0453/9799/9783/files/KAST-O-LITE_30_LI_PLUS_data.pdf - Dense high-duty firebrick density about 134 pcf and conductivity about 1.2 to 1.4 W/mK: Jet D.P. item.title: 006. What a Feynman diagram is
item.description:
- A Feynman diagram is one term in a perturbation series for a scattering amplitude: external lines are particle states, internal lines are propagators, each vertex is a factor of the coupling, and free loop momenta are integrated over. In QED each extra loop costs another power of the fine-structure constant (about 1/137), so the series is useful. - The showcase is the electron's magnetic moment: Schwinger's one-loop alpha/2pi (1947-48), then 7, 72, 891 and 12,672 diagrams at two to five loops. The 2023 Northwestern measurement (0.13 parts per trillion) agrees with theory to about one part in 10^12, conditional on which measured value of alpha is used. - The positron-as-backward-electron idea (Stueckelberg 1941, Feynman 1949) is a reading of the math. The arrow tracks electron-number (charge) flow, and a diagram fixes neither a trajectory nor a time order. Diagrams spread by apprenticeship (Kaiser) and fail where the coupling is not small, such as low-energy QCD.
Chew on this: 1. If a single diagram can be reshuffled by changing a convention but the sum can't, what does it mean to say a particular diagram "dominates" a process? Is that a statement about the world or about the bookkeeping? 2. Experiment, theory and the value of alpha are tied in a knot of three. If the cesium and rubidium values stay apart, how would you decide which side of the knot is wrong? 3. Smiths got steel right for millennia without the theory, and physicists get predictions right with a series they believe doesn't converge. Is there a real difference between a craft that works without knowing why and a calculation that works while knowing it strictly shouldn't?
Sources: - Measured g/2 with 0.13 ppt uncertainty, 2.2 times better than 2008, agreement to 1 part in 10^12, Cs and Rb alpha discrepancy, alpha from g: Fan, Myers, Sukra, Gabrielse, "Measurement of the Electron Magnetic Moment," Phys. Rev. Lett. (2023), arXiv 2209.13084: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2209.13084 - Five-loop result: 12,672 diagrams, 891 at four loops, coefficient 9.16(58), automated code generation and numerical integration, agreement with experiment: Aoyama, Hayakawa, Kinoshita, Nio, "Tenth-Order QED Contribution to the Electron g-2," Phys. Rev. Lett. 109, 111807 (2012), arXiv 1205.5368: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1205.5368 - Schwinger's alpha/2pi (end of 1947), Kusch and Foley, diagram counts 1, 7, 72, 891, 12,672, higher orders at least a hundred times smaller, Dyson's divergence argument and the asymptotic-series view: Ivan Todorov, "From Euler's play with infinite series to the anomalous magnetic moment," arXiv 1804.09553 (2018): https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.09553 - Fine-structure constant, 1/137.035 999 177 (CODATA 2022): Particle Data Group, Physical Constants table (2025): https://pdg.lbl.gov/2025/reviews/rpp2025-rev-phys-constants.pdf - Vertex factor proportional to the electron charge, two vertices at tree level, virtual particles off the mass shell, arrows showing particle flow, internal lines integrated over all space and time so a diagram includes all time orderings: Oxford teaching handout, "Feynman diagrams" (AJB, 2011): https://users.ox.ac.uk/~dpmp0180/teaching/feynman.pdf - Fermion arrows point along particle flow and backwards for antiparticles; time order not important: Mike Birse, University of Manchester, PHYS 30121 notes on Feynman diagrams: https://www.theory.physics.manchester.ac.uk/~mikeb/lecture/phys30121/feynman.pdf - The case for and against virtual particles (Falkenburg, Teller, Weingard, Fox), conclusion that they are as real as other quantum particles: Gregg Jaeger, "Are Virtual Particles Less Real?", Entropy 21(2), 2019: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7514619 - item.title: 005. The gas fire, part 1: combustion
item.description:
- Propane carries about 2.5 times the energy of natural gas per cubic foot (about 2,488 vs 1,012 Btu) and needs about 2.5 times the air (23.7 vs 9.6 cubic feet), so both need about the same air per Btu (Thornton's rule); adiabatic flame temperatures differ by tens of degrees, not hundreds, and laminar flame speeds are similar and slow (about 36 to 42 cm/s). - A venturi burner's only pump is the momentum of the gas jet, which scales with supply pressure: a propane regulator at 10 psi gives about 40 times the push of household gas at about 7 inches of water column, and a forge needs nearly all its air premixed, so low-pressure natural gas usually wants a blower. - Rich, neutral and lean set how much free oxygen, carbon monoxide and hydrogen surround the bar; even a neutral flame scales steel above about 750 C because of its CO2 and water vapor; dragon's breath is CO and H2 from a rich fire burning in room air; scale is about 95% wüstite, which grows fast because iron diffuses outward through its vacancies (parabolic law).
Forge task: Cut two identical pieces of mild steel from the same bar (for example a few inches of 3/8 by 1 inch flat). Wire-brush them clean and weigh each to 0.1 g. Run the forge lean (choke open, or gas turned down against the air on a blown burner) until there is no flame at the door; let it settle ten minutes. Give the first piece ten minutes by a timer at a full yellow forging heat in a marked spot, then let it cool untouched. Set the forge rich (a few inches of orange to yellow flame at the door), let it settle, and repeat with the second piece in the same spot for the same time. Compare surfaces cold, then knock and brush off the scale and reweigh. The mass lost is scale loss, lean vs rich.
Safety: carbon monoxide alarm installed and tested before you light; doors open and air moving, especially on the rich run, which makes the most carbon monoxide. Leak-test every fitting with soapy water, never a flame. On a small propane bottle, watch for frost and stop if the forge sags; never warm a bottle with a torch or by the forge. Safety glasses when knocking off scale. Keep sparks and ignition sources away from low spots where propane would collect.
Chew on this: 1. If the air needed per Btu is nearly the same for every hydrocarbon, what does that say about where the energy in burning comes from, and is there a fuel you might forge with that breaks the rule? 2. Steel mills fire rich around the steel and burn the leftovers with extra air downstream. Could you build that into a hobby forge, and what would it cost in heat and in carbon monoxide? 3. item.title: 004. Bloomery to Bessemer
item.description:
- For most of history steel was made without knowing carbon existed: the bloomery reduced ore in the solid state and gave an uneven bloom of soft iron, steel and phosphoric iron that smiths sorted by hand; cementation soaked carbon into bars over days; crucible steel (South Asian wootz, Central Asian crucible steel, Huntsman's Sheffield cast steel) evened it out by melting. - The blast furnace went the other way, loading iron with about 4% carbon so it melts near 1130 C, and puddling burned the carbon back out; carbon was proposed as the difference between iron, steel and cast iron around 1781 to 1786 and took decades to become consensus. - Bessemer (1856) burned the carbon out with air, using the impurities as fuel; Mushet's manganese dealt with oxide and sulfur (the hot-shortness link to the smithing track), and the Thomas-Gilchrist basic lining (1878-79) finally removed phosphorus.
Chew on this: 1. The wootz makers forged cool and cycled the steel many times, and the pattern only appears if you don't overheat it. What other craft practices might encode a phase boundary, a temperature you must not cross, without anyone having named it? 2. Swedish iron was a trusted brand long before anyone could say why it was better. What would you test before trusting a steel supplier the way Sheffield trusted Dannemora? 3. The Damascus nanotube story spread far faster than the correction. What's your checklist for deciding whether a striking claim about old technology is replicated or just repeated?

item.title: 003. Why steel moves, part 2: where it goes wrong
item.description:
- Hot shortness: sulfur collects at grain boundaries as iron sulfide, and the iron/iron-sulfide eutectic melts at about 988 C, inside the forging range, so boundaries go liquid under the hammer. Manganese ties sulfur up as manganese sulfide (melts about 1610 C) in discrete inclusions. Copper from scrap causes a separate hot shortness that manganese doesn't fix. - Blue brittleness (roughly 200 to 370 C by the glossaries) is dynamic strain aging: carbon and nitrogen pin moving dislocations, raising strength and cutting ductility below room-temperature levels; the trough moves hotter as you strike faster. Grain growth is driven by boundary energy, accelerates sharply with temperature, costs toughness, and is reset by the phase change in normalizing; overheated steel recovers, burnt steel doesn't. - Glow color is the visible tail of black-body radiation, so it tracks temperature steeply but is judged against ambient light. The magnet mostly tracks the transformation to austenite, not the Curie point (about 770 C); the Curie point only governs low-carbon steels, and the magnet says nothing about carbide dissolution in hypereutectoid steels or full transformation in chromium-alloyed ones. Recalescence is the visible release of transformation heat on cooling.
Forge task: In a dimmed shop, heat a finger-sized bar of known high-carbon steel (1084 or 1095) evenly to a little past nonmagnetic, check with a magnet, and hold a minute. Lay it on a firebrick out of drafts and watch it cool through dull red: it dims, then briefly flushes brighter, often as a traveling band. That is recalescence. Test with the magnet just before and just after. Optionally heat a second bar slowly and watch through the forge mouth for a darker patch lagging as it crosses critical (decalescence).
Safety: safety glasses against scale, and don't stare into the forge mouth for long. Leak-test gas fittings with soapy water, never a flame. If you close up the shop to darken it, keep ventilation running and the carbon monoxide alarm on; the forge still makes CO. Propane pools low; natural gas rises. No galvanized, plated or leaded stock in the fire.
Chew on this: 1. Sulfur is still in your steel as manganese sulfide stringers stretched along the bar by rolling. What would you expect for toughness along the bar versus across it? 2. If you moved your forge from a dim garage to a bright, open shop, which way would your heats drift before you noticed, and how would you catch it? 3. If a normalize resets grain size anyway, why does the last forging heat matter so much, and what does that say about when to stop forging and start heat treating?

item.title: 002. Time's arrow
item.description:
- The fundamental laws are time-reversal invariant for practical purposes (the weak-force T violation BaBar observed directly in 2012 is real but tidy, CPT survives, and it is not known to have anything to do with the everyday arrow); Boltzmann's 1877 counting argument, S = k log W over coarse-grained macrostates, explains entropy increase as overwhelming odds, not necessity. - Loschmidt's reversibility objection, pushed to its end, shows that counting alone also predicts a higher-entropy past; the fix is a boundary condition, Albert's "Past Hypothesis", and Boltzmann's alternative (we live in a fluctuation) fails on the Boltzmann brain problem. - The early universe was thermally near-equilibrium but gravitationally smooth, which with gravity is the low-entropy state (Penrose; Egan and Lineweaver's budget runs from about 10^89 k in radiation to about 10^104 k today, mostly in supermassive black holes, against a ceiling near 10^122 to 10^123 k); the radiative arrow probably reduces to the thermodynamic one, the records and causal arrows only partly, the cosmological arrow does not flip in recollapse, and why the Past Hypothesis holds is open.
Chew on this: 1. The second law is statistics, and small systems break it for short times. How small and how short before "never seen" becomes "seen sometimes", and does that change what you mean by "law"? 2. If records depend on a low-entropy past, a record of the future would need a low-entropy future. Is anything in physics like that, and is our inability to remember tomorrow a fact about brains or about the cosmos? 3. The Past Hypothesis is a law, a brute accident, or something deeper theory will explain. Which would satisfy you, and what evidence could tell them apart?

item.title: 001. Why steel moves, part 1: the lattice
item.description:
- Steel bends because dislocations, line defects in the crystal, glide one atomic row at a time; that is why real iron yields at roughly 1/500 of a perfect crystal's theoretical strength. - Face-centered austenite has 12 close-packed slip systems and body-centered ferrite has awkward, thermally activated screw dislocations, but at forging heat temperature matters more than lattice, and the evidence found suggests austenite is if anything the harder phase at the same temperature. - Hot work doesn't work-harden because recovery and recrystallization clean up dislocations as fast as the hammer makes them (austenite mainly by dynamic recrystallization, ferrite by dynamic recovery); "too cold to forge" is where that cleanup stops keeping up, and a hammer's fast blows act "colder" and work the surface where a press works the whole section.
Forge task: Saturday morning, walk the shop with a notebook and list everything between you and lighting the forge. Don't fix anything yet. Check: propane bottle fill and date, regulator and hose condition, forge lining, anvil access, a clear path forge to anvil to quench, extinguisher present and charged.
Safety: leak-test every gas fitting with soapy water before any flame, never with a lighter. Put a carbon monoxide alarm in the shop if there isn't one. Pull anything galvanized or plated out of the scrap pile so it never ends up in the fire.
Chew on this: 1. If austenite recrystallizes whenever it's worked hard and hot, the finished grain size should depend mostly on the last heat and last few blows. Does that match your experience, and what does it mean for how you finish a piece? 2. Would a press-forged and a hammer-forged bar of the same steel differ inside, and how would you find out? 3. "FCC forges easily" was a working rule with a slightly wrong reason. What other shop lore might be right in practice and wrong in explanation?

first TEM sighting 1955-56 by Hirsch's group: University of Kiel, "Heroes of Dislocation Science": https://www.tf.uni-kiel.de/matwis/amat/iss/kap_5/advanced/t5_4_1.html - FCC slip, 12 systems with 5 independent, no close-packed plane in BCC, Schmid's law, von Mises criterion, work hardening and Lomer locks: DoITPoMS, Slip in Single Crystals: https://www.doitpoms.ac.uk/tlplib/slip/printall.php - Perfect-crystal vs dislocation stress estimates (about G/5 vs G/180): DoITPoMS, Introduction to Dislocations: https://www.doitpoms.ac.uk/tlplib/dislocations/printall.php - FCC {111} planes, <110> directions, 12 systems: University of Washington MSE 170, Lecture 10: https://courses.washington.edu/mse170/lecture_notes/rolandiF08/Lecture10-MR2008.pdf - Thermally activated screw dislocation glide and kink-pair mechanism in BCC iron: Screw dislocation modelling in BCC iron, npj Computational Materials (2018): https://www.nature.com/articles/s41524-018-0125-4 - Iron allotropes (912, 1394, 1538 C), carbon solubility in ferrite and austenite, Curie point: Wikipedia, Allotropes of iron: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allotropes_of_iron - Austenite as the harder phase in hot working;
